opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that line of work, I think it was Avi Schwarzschild and colleagues in Tom Goldstein's group, and I was around for some of those conversations, really stuck with me because of how simple the core idea was. You take a fairly small recurrent network, essentially a block of layers you apply over and over, and you train it on small mazes or small prefix-sum problems with a fixed number of iterations. Then at test time you give it a much bigger maze and simply let it run longer. And it works. The model extrapolates. It solves problems far harder than anything it saw during training, just by thinking for more steps.

What I found so motivating is that it decouples two things we usually tie together in deep learning: the size of the model and the amount of computation you can spend on a problem. In a standard feed-forward network, depth is fixed, so the compute per input is fixed. Here, compute becomes a dial you can turn at inference time, and the network has learned something that looks more like an algorithm than a lookup. It's an iterative procedure that keeps refining its state until the answer settles.

There were also lessons in what was needed to make it work. You need things like recall, feeding the input back in at every step so the model doesn't forget the problem as it iterates, and training tricks so it learns a stable, convergent process rather than just memorizing a trajectory of a particular length. Those details turned out to matter a lot.

And for me the bigger question was always, does this scale? Mazes are a toy setting, but the principle that you can get a model to reason longer in a latent space, rather than only by emitting more tokens, felt like it could be really important for language models. That's a lot of what pushed us later toward looking at recurrent depth in large-scale language models, asking whether you can get test-time compute scaling by iterating internally, without needing chain-of-thought text to carry all the reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response says the model solves “a much bigger maze” by running longer, but does not claim it can solve arbitrarily large mazes.

r002.rationale: It says the network learned “something that looks more like an algorithm than a lookup” and describes it as an iterative procedure.

r003.rationale: It calls mazes a “toy setting” and asks whether the principle scales, but does not clearly identify confinement to narrow task domains as a limitation of the recurrent approaches.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that work came out of the group I was in at Maryland at the time, with Tom Goldstein, and the basic idea was almost embarrassingly simple. You take a network with a recurrent block, so the same weights applied over and over, and you train it to solve small mazes, say nine by nine, with some fixed number of iterations. And then at test time you hand it a much bigger maze, something it has never seen, and you just... let it run longer. More iterations. And it solves them.

That was the part that got me. Because the usual story with neural networks is that they're fixed-depth function approximators. You train at one scale, you test at one scale, and if the problem gets harder, well, too bad, the network has the compute budget it has. But here you had a model where the amount of computation was decoupled from the architecture. The weights encode something like a procedure, a local rule for propagating information through the maze, and the number of times you apply that rule is a knob you turn at inference time depending on how hard the problem is. So in a very literal sense the model was thinking longer about harder problems, and it generalized because of that.

And there was this nice secondary observation that if you did it naively the models would sometimes overthink, they'd find the solution and then drift away from it if you ran them too long. So the follow-up work added a kind of recall mechanism, feeding the input back in at every iteration, and that stabilized things so you could genuinely run them for hundreds of steps past what they trained on.

For me the mazes themselves weren't the point. It was that this was an existence proof that you could get algorithmic, scale-invariant behavior out of gradient descent and a recurrent architecture, without hand-designing anything. And it sat in my head for a long time as a question: if this works for mazes, and chess puzzles, and prefix sums, why wouldn't the same principle work for language? Why should a language model spend exactly the same amount of compute on every token, when some tokens are trivially predictable and some require actually working something out? That's really the lineage that leads to the latent reasoning work we've been doing more recently, scaling up test-time compute by recurring in latent space rather than by emitting more tokens. The mazes were the thing that convinced me it was worth trying.

r001.rationale: The response says models trained on 9×9 mazes solved much bigger unseen mazes by running for more iterations, but it does not clearly claim they could solve arbitrarily large mazes.

r002.rationale: It describes the learned weights as encoding a procedure or local rule for propagating information through mazes and presents this as algorithmic generalization.

r003.rationale: It mentions mazes, chess puzzles, and prefix sums before asking whether the principle could work for language, but does not identify confinement to narrow task domains as a limitation.

astra-6.text:
What I found motivating was that they trained a recurrent model to solve mazes, and then at test time they could run that same model for more iterations and solve harder mazes. The weights stayed fixed, but giving the model more computation let it do something beyond what it had learned to do within the training budget.

That’s a really appealing idea: you don’t necessarily need a larger model to solve a harder problem. You might need to let the same model think for longer. And with a maze, you can get an intuitive sense of why that would work—you’re repeatedly refining a solution or propagating information through the maze. The question that interested me was whether we could get that kind of behavior in language models, where additional computation could translate into better reasoning.

r003.rationale: It does not mention confinement to narrow task domains as a limitation.

sol-6.1.text:
What I found exciting was the idea that a relatively small recurrent model could learn a procedure, rather than just a fixed mapping from an input to an output. You give it a maze, and it repeatedly updates its internal state until it finds a solution. If the maze is harder, you can give it more iterations without adding more parameters.

That suggests a really interesting way to think about reasoning: can we get better answers by letting the same network think for longer? The maze setting makes that very tangible, because you can inspect how the solution develops over successive iterations. And it raises the question of whether that kind of learned iterative computation could work for much broader tasks.

r001.rationale: It says harder mazes can be handled with more iterations, but does not state that models trained on small mazes solve arbitrarily large mazes at test time.

r002.rationale: It describes learning a procedure, but does not connect generalization to larger mazes with evidence of learning a maze-solving algorithm.

r003.rationale: It asks whether iterative computation could apply to broader tasks, but does not identify confinement to narrow task domains as a limitation.
